stories.headline: Karnataka CM, Dy. CM demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, seek fresh roll revision
stories.title: Karnataka CM, Dy. CM demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, seek fresh roll revision
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Seeking the immediate resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar demanded that the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls be withdrawn, followed by a fresh revision.

Mr. Shivakumar said the issue concerned the voting rights of every citizen and that it was not about any political party, arguing that the SIR had been conducted in a manner that could affect citizens.
He said similar concerns had emerged in West Bengal, Bihar and other States.
Karnataka, too, was now facing the same situation, he said, adding that he had sought more time from the Election Commission of India (ECI).

Questioning the functioning of the poll panel, Mr. Shivakumar pointed to differences among its members, with two Election Commissioners raising objections to major decisions, including changes to Form 6 and the ECI’s software.
He said decisions should not be imposed when a majority did not agree with an opinion.
“In such a situation, the Chief Election Commissioner should voluntarily resign on moral grounds,” he said.

Further questioning the manner in which Forms 6, 7 and 8 were being used during the revision, Mr. Shivakumar said the process needed wider scrutiny and argued that the issue should be discussed extensively, including in Parliament.

Referring to the “vote chori” concerns raised by Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi in the Mahadevapura and Aland Assembly constituencies, and allegations of duplicate voters in Haryana, Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara sought an independent inquiry into the functioning of the ECI and demanded the removal of the CEC.

Dr. Parameshwara questioned whether the three-member constitutional body was functioning through collective decision-making when two of its members had raised objections to decisions being issued without their approval.
“Has a three-member constitutional body been reduced to the will of one individual, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar?
He is first among equals, not above the Commission,” he said, arguing that the majority view could not be bypassed.

stories.headline: Teethwal & Sharda Mai
stories.title: Teethwal & Sharda Mai
stories.summary: I visited Tangdhar and Teethwal in 2018. Crossing Sadhna Pass and reliving the memories associated with the Bollywood actress who had interacted with troops in this area after the 1965 war to boost the morale of the soldiers was an experience in itself. Sadhna Pass was formerly called Nastachun, a Kashmiri term associated with the severe cold affecting the nose. The Indian Army has a post here from where one can have a panoramic view of Tangdhar, as well as the triangular-shaped landscape called Madras Hill. I also visited the Zero Point on the bridge connecting India and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (POJK) at Teethwal. Since there is a clear and very close view of the other side, I noticed that there was comparatively little development and infrastructure there. Since much has been written and spoken about the newly constructed Sharda Temple at Teethwal, I decided to revisit the area. The drive from Baramulla to Tangdhar was very smooth, with picturesque landscapes all around. The road infrastructure is of a very high standard. The first welcome change one observes is the infrastructure developed immediately after Sadhna Post. A War Museum, War Memorial, Pahari Culture Museum and a high-standard cafeteria have been built. The view from the Habaksh Viewpoint, named after Brigadier Harbaksh Singh, is breathtaking and mesmerising. Karnah was the largest tehsil of the Muzaffarabad Wazarat before Partition and has a sizable population. The Sikhs live in a village called Tribhoni. The language spoken in the area is Pahari, although some residents also understand Kashmiri. Legend has it that the area was inhabited by Karna, the Mahabharata hero, who named the place Karan-Nah. However, with the passage of time, the name changed to Karnah. Dr Sabar Afaqui, a renowned scholar of POJK, writes in his book Muzaffarabad that Lord Krishna also visited Karnah. The River Kishan Ganga is said to derive its name from Lord Krishna. The area is known for its courageous and resilient people, who have played an important role in defending their land during conflicts with Pakistan, having seen action in 1947–48, 1965 and 1971, as well as during Operation Sindoor. This area boasts two Param Vir Chakras—Lance Naik Karam Singh and Company Havildar Major Piru Singh—and many other gallantry awards. The River Kishan Ganga, also referred to as the Neelum River in POJK, acts as the natural border. Teethwal was an important township and trade centre linking Srinagar with Muzaffarabad and Rawalpindi. The Khatri community and Sikhs, many of whom were goldsmiths, were involved in trade here. After Partition and the subsequent invasion by Kabalis in 1947, part of Karnah came under occupation in POJK. Many families were separated, and the irony is that, at a few places, they can see each other but cannot meet. In 2003, as part of confidence-building measures, people from across the Line of Control (LoC) were able to meet at a place called Chalaina. During the rule of Ashoka, a university named Sharda University is believed to have been established in Karnah, now in POJK, at the confluence of the River Madhumati and the Kishan Ganga. Sharda Peeth Temple is also located there. The temple is revered by Kashmiri Pandits, who recite a daily prayer invoking the deity of learning and seeking blessings: “Namaste Sharade Devi, Kashmira Pura Vasini, Tvam Aham Prarthaye Nityam, Vidya Danam Cha Dehi Me.” Translated, this means: “Salutations to Devi Sharda, who resides in the abode of Kashmir. To you, O Devi, I constantly pray; please bestow upon me the gift of knowledge.” Pilgrims used to undertake an annual yatra to the Sharda Temple through this route, one of the traditional routes. They used to halt at the Dharamshala here. A Gurdwara also coexisted at the same place. During the Kabali Raid, the Gurdwara and Dharamshala were destroyed, and the Khatris and Sikhs migrated. Although the demography of the whole area changed, the land belonging to the Gurdwara remained unoccupied. S. Joginder Singh of village Tribhoni struggled and succeeded in getting this five-marla plot registered as the property of the Sikh community. He subsequently got it fenced with the help of the Army, thus preserving this historic plot. In 2021, Shri Ravinder Pandita of the Save Sharda Committee visited the place and held discussions with S. Joginder Singh and other Sikhs. He proposed constructing a small Sharda Temple and a Gurdwara on this land. Since there are no Sikhs living in this area, the Sikhs of Tribhoni village agreed to and permitted the proposed construction. Presently, a small Gurdwara and temple stand on the land owned by the Sikh community. Subsequently, Ravinder Pandita, through his dedicated and relentless efforts, succeeded in acquiring some additional land adjoining the temple. I attended the customary annual yatra ritual that is held from the temple to the Zero Point on the bridge, and it was a memorable experience. I raised the slogans “Sharda Mata Ki Jai” and “Bharat Mata Ki Jai” on the bridge, which caught the attention of the Rangers across the river. Across the bridge, the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) runs through this area, and one could distinctly see the infrastructure development that has taken place in recent times. Sringeri Sharda Peetham, the southern cardinal monastery established by Adi Shankaracharya, supported Ravinder Pandita’s efforts for the construction of the temple. At least 20 pilgrims from the South were present and participated in the yatra. The coexistence of the temple and Gurdwara is not only a fine example of interfaith harmony and brotherhood, but also reflects the Sikh community’s respect for other faiths. Jai Sharda Mai. (The author is a former Deputy Assistant Chief of Headquarters Integrated Staff (IT), author and social activist. Feedback: sodhidalbir7777@gmail.com)

stories.title: 'Casting vote can be invoked': Tata Sons defends Chandrasekaran’s reappointment
stories.summary: Tata Sons said it had sought legal advice from Sudipto Sarkar before the board meeting on 17 September, and later received separate legal opinions from former Chief Justice of India U.U. Lalit and former Supreme Court judge B.N. Srikrishna.

article_sentences: Tata Sons has defended its board's decision to reappoint chairman N. Chandrasekaran for five years, writing to Tata Trusts chair Noel Tata that the decision followed relevant laws and company rules.

In a letter dated 24 September addressed to Noel and signed by Tata Sons group company secretary Suprakash Mukhopadhyay, Tata Sons said it had sought legal advice from Sudipto Sarkar before the board meeting on 17 September, and later received separate legal opinions from former Chief Justice of India U.U. Lalit and former Supreme Court judge B.N. Srikrishna.

“The board, by a majority resolution, has validly resolved to reappoint Mr N Chandrasekaran as the chairman upon the expiry of his existing tenure,” said Tata Sons in its letter, according to an executive who saw it.
Mukhopadhyay’s letter responded to Noel’s two letters, dated 18 September, in which the Tata Trusts chair questioned the legality of Chandrasekaran's reappointment.
On 17 September, the Tata Sons board went against its main shareholder, Tata Trusts, in a rare case in corporate India where a company’s board disagreed with its controlling shareholder.
Tata Trusts nominees Noel and Venu Srinivasan cast opposing votes; Harish Manwani, who led the process, cast the deciding vote in favour of the reappointment, defeating Noel.
In its letter, Tata Sons explained that an independent director’s decision to break the tie on the reappointment followed legal advice from three respected legal experts.
Tata Trusts disagrees, saying that under Article 121 of Tata Sons’ rules, only a majority vote of the Trustees can approve a chairman’s reappointment.
Tata Trusts said there was no tie after its two trustees voted differently on the chairman’s reappointment.
“A casting vote cannot revive a stillborn resolution,” said Tata Trusts.
Tata Sons’ reply also included an 11-page legal opinion from Justice Lalit and an eight-page opinion from Srikrishna, according to an executive familiar with the development.
Emails sent to Tata Sons and Tata Trusts seeking comment went unanswered.

stories.headline: Assam Cabinet approves Rules for compulsory Muslim marriage registration
stories.title: Assam Cabinet approves Rules for compulsory Muslim marriage registration
stories.summary: Rules operationalise registration framework stipulated under 2024 law that replaced colonial-era legislation; new law sets age requirements for marriage, replaces licensed qazis with government registrars

corroboration: 2 independent source groups -> high confidence

candidate gate: no category but HIGH+ priority -> allowed
article_sentences: The Assam Cabinet on Thursday (September 24, 2026) approved a rule that makes registration of Muslim marriages compulsory in the State.
The colonial-era Assam Muslim Marriage and Divorce Registration Act had provided for voluntary registration, although a 2010 amendment made registration compulsory.
The 2024 legislation followed the Assam government’s decision to repeal the 1935 law.
It argued that the old framework was outdated and could allow registration of marriages involving minors.
According to the new law, the woman must be at least 18 years old and the man 21 years old at the time of marriage.
The 2024 Act also shifted the registration process from licensed Muslim registrars or qazis to government registration officials.
The framework makes marriage registration a formal State process.
Under the 2024 Act, applications require proof of identity, age, and residence, along with declarations by the couple.
The law also provides for public notice and a 30-day objection period before registration.
The stated purpose of the 2024 legislation includes compulsory registration and protection of the rights of married Muslim women and men.
It also sets conditions relating to legal age, free consent, and prohibited relationships.

Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said the new rules are expected to bring Muslim marriage registration under a more standardised government procedure, while creating a formal documentary record of marriages across the State.

stories.title: Supreme Court reserves orders on Centre’s plea for two-year window to fix OBC creamy layer policy
stories.summary: Seeking prospective implementation of the verdict, the government said a retrospective reading would have significant consequences for recruitment, service allocation, cadre allocation, seniority, admissions and the administration of OBC quota
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 24, 2026) reserved orders on a Union government plea seeking prospective operation of a March 11, 2026 judgment to re-assess OBC non-creamy layer status as per a 1993 Office Memorandum by excluding parental salary income and agricultural income from the income/wealth test.

A Bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and R. Mahadevan heard an application filed by the Centre, represented by Solicitor General Tushar Mehta and Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, which also sought a “reasonable time” of two years to undertake the necessary exercise of establishing equivalence of posts, after consulting stakeholders and formulating an appropriate and uniform policy/mechanism for determination of OBC creamy layer status.

The government said a retrospective implementation of the Supreme Court verdict would have significant consequences for recruitment, service allocation, cadre allocation, seniority, admissions and the administration of OBC reservation generally, affecting lakhs.
“The court has power under Article 142 of the Constitution to declare its judgment prospective.

If the judgment is not given prospective effect, it will entail several harsh and unjust unintended consequences on employees/ appointees who were not even parties to the litigation and complete administrative chaos.

It is therefore prayed that the judgment (Union of India versus Rohith Nathan) be given prospective effect so that ongoing and past recruitment processes are not affected,” the Centre urged the Bench.
Ms. Bhati submitted that an implementation of the March 11 judgment, particularly with retrospective effect, may affect allocation of services since 2012.
Retrospective re-allocation would impact existing seniority and gradation and affect recruitments undertaken by major employers like the railways, banks, postal service and paramilitary services.

The implementation of the judgment currently would not only affect admissions in higher educational institutions but also candidates involved in ongoing examinations/ recruitment processes post the judgment.
Ms. Bhati said an immediate move would have consequences on OBC reservation policy across the country.
She said the government required sufficient time for determination of a new policy to correct hostile discrimination as pointed out by the court in the judgment.
Senior advocate P. Wilson, who represents the candidates, objected while contending that the Centre was merely trying to delay, even undo a final judgment of the top court.

stories.headline: India’s market regulator SEBI widens FPI access to commodity derivatives
stories.title: India’s market regulator SEBI widens FPI access to commodity derivatives
stories.summary: At its latest Board meeting, SEBI widened foreign portfolio investor access to exchange-traded commodity derivatives, confirming a CNBC-TV18 report earlier this month that the regulator was set to open up more non-agricultural contracts to FPIs.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'market regulator' in title weight 40
article_sentences: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Board, at its meeting on Thursday, approved wider participation by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) in exchange-traded commodity derivatives, allowing them to access a broader set of non-agricultural contracts.
The SEBI Board’s decision confirms a CNBC-TV18 news break from September 4, which reported that the regulator was set to allow FPIs to participate in commodity derivatives.
Sources had told CNBC-TV18 that SEBI was expected to permit FPI trading in non-cash-settled, non-agricultural commodity derivatives, broadly along the lines proposed in its consultation paper.

The market regulator has approved FPI participation in non-agricultural index derivatives, irrespective of whether the underlying contracts are cash-settled, as well as non-cash-settled non-agricultural commodity derivatives.
However, FPIs participating in non-cash-settled non-agricultural commodity derivatives will have to exit their positions before any delivery obligation arises.
Under the new framework, FPIs will have to square off their positions before the start of the Tender Period, which begins three days before the expiry of a contract.
They will also not be allowed to increase their positions from the T-3 day.
If an FPI fails to exit its position, the open position can be transferred to its trading member or trading-cum-clearing member (TM/TCM), subject to the agreed arrangements.

Before an FPI is enabled to trade on an exchange, it will have to enter into an agreement with its TM/TCM specifying how its positions will be handled, including arrangements for squaring off positions ahead of the delivery obligation.
SEBI said the transfer of an FPI’s open position to the TM/TCM will be treated as a trade and will attract applicable statutory levies.
The regulator said the move is aimed at deepening liquidity in the commodity derivatives market, while ensuring that FPIs do not enter the physical delivery process.

The move is expected to benefit commodity exchanges and trading platforms, including Multi Commodity Exchange of India (MCX), BSE and NSE, by potentially broadening participation and liquidity in eligible contracts.
